kubectl annotate deploy app meta.helm.sh/release-name=app meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=prod --overwrite
tip: Say diff until it's boring, then adopt.

q: What are common Helm anti-patterns and best practices you would enforce in code review?
a: Anti-patterns I flag include hard-coded values and names in templates; deep logic and long conditionals that make templates unreadable; forking third-party charts instead of customising through values or post-renderers; floating versions such as latest tags or unpinned dependency ranges; storing secrets in values files; using reuse-values or ad-hoc set flags in production so state cannot be reproduced; changing selectors or resource names between versions; missing resource requests, probes and security contexts; huge umbrella charts that couple unrelated services; hooks used for long-running or non-idempotent work; no schema, tests or documentation; and publishing charts without bumping versions. Best practices are the opposite: follow the recommended label conventions and the fullname helper; make values a documented, validated interface with a schema and safe defaults; keep templates simple, factoring helpers; pin chart and image versions, preferably digests; run lint, kubeconform, policy checks, unit and install tests, and helm diff in CI; deploy with atomic, wait and timeouts; keep values and chart versions in Git with GitOps; handle CRDs deliberately; and write upgrade notes for breaking changes. A short checklist in the pull request template turns these into habit.
f: Why is forking upstream charts discouraged?
Which flags make production deploys safer?
p: Avoid hard-coded values, complex templates, forks, floating versions, secrets in values, reuse-values, unstable selectors, missing limits and probes, hooks for heavy work and untested charts. Enforce schema, tests, diffs, pinned versions and digests, atomic deploys and GitOps, with a review checklist.
cmds: helm lint . --strict && helm unittest . && helm template . | kubeconform -strict
tip: Say simple templates, pinned versions, tested upgrades.

q: How do you handle breaking changes when upgrading a major chart version, for example a third-party chart that renamed values?
a: I treat a major chart upgrade as a small project. First read the changelog and upgrade notes for removed or renamed values, changed defaults, new minimum Kubernetes or dependency versions, CRD changes and required manual steps. Then fetch both chart versions and diff the default values and templates to see everything that changes. In a staging environment that mirrors production, back up data, and run the upgrade with my existing values plus the diff plugin, which shows the real Kubernetes-level changes: selector changes that will fail as immutable, recreated stateful sets, removed resources, and changed images. Update my values files to the new keys, using the schema or lint errors to catch leftovers, and apply any manual steps such as CRD upgrades through kubectl first. Where it is risky, use a maintenance window, a blue-green approach by installing the new chart version alongside the old one and migrating data, or step through intermediate versions if the notes require it. Verify with smoke tests and metrics, and keep a rollback plan, remembering data migrations may not be reversible. Document the outcome for other environments, then promote in order.
f: Why diff both chart versions?
When use blue-green for a major chart upgrade?
p: Read upgrade notes, diff default values and templates between versions, rehearse in staging with backups and helm diff, update renamed values, apply CRD steps manually, consider intermediate versions or blue-green for risky changes, verify with tests and promote with a rollback plan.
cmds: helm pull repo/chart --version 14.0.0 --untar --untardir new && helm pull repo/chart --version 13.5.2 --untar --untardir old && diff -ru old new | less
helm diff upgrade app repo/chart --version 14.0.0 -f values.yaml
tip: Say rehearse in staging with diff and backups.

q: How do you build and use Helm OCI dependencies and chart caching in air-gapped or restricted environments?
a: Air-gapped clusters cannot reach public registries, so everything is mirrored and resolved internally. The process starts in a connected staging area where approved charts and images are pulled, scanned and reviewed, then copied into an internal OCI registry with tools such as helm pull and helm push, oras, skopeo or crane, or a registry replication feature in Harbor, preserving versions and digests. Chart dependencies in Chart.yaml point at the internal registry, so dependency build resolves offline, and Chart.lock keeps exact versions. Image references in values are rewritten to the internal registry, using global image registry values, or a post-renderer, or a mirror configured on the container runtime. For a fully disconnected network, charts and images are exported into a signed bundle, transferred over an approved medium, verified against signatures and digests, then imported. Vendoring dependency archives in Git removes registry reliance for builds. The Helm cache and config directories in CI are set to known paths, so runs are reproducible without network calls. Updates follow a regular cadence with the same scan and approval steps, and an inventory records which versions are present.
f: How do images get rewritten to the internal registry?
What verifies a transferred bundle?
p: Mirror reviewed charts and images into an internal OCI registry, point dependencies and image values at it, keep Chart.lock and vendored archives for offline builds, transfer signed bundles for fully disconnected networks, verify digests and signatures and refresh on a regular approved cadence.
cmds: helm pull oci://public.example/charts/app --version 1.4.0 && helm push app-1.4.0.tgz oci://registry.internal/charts
tip: Say mirror, pin, verify, rewrite image registries.
